spots.name: Vilnius University
spots.label: Vilnius University

text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In Vilnius, Lithuania's capital, where the university buildings and grounds spread over an area about 300 metres across.
text.description: Vilnius University is the oldest and largest university in Lithuania, and on the map it works as a whole cluster of university grounds rather than a single building. The outline of the site is about 300 metres across, so there is plenty to explore on foot. It was founded in 1579 as the Jesuit Academy of Vilnius by Stephen Báthory, which makes it one of the older universities in Central and Eastern Europe. It was closed after the failed November Uprising of 1830–1831 and did not reopen until 1919. Today more than 23,000 students study here, and the university also runs a library, a museum and botanical gardens. For a phone photographer the appeal is the sense of age and scale: long façades, passages and open courtyards where you can include people walking through to show size. Take a few wide frames to set the scene, then move closer for doors, windows, stonework and signs. Walk slowly and look for places where one building frames another. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep vertical walls straight, and check for passing students or visitors before you press the shutter. This is a working university, so respect any signs and access rules.
text.access_note: This is a working university, so respect any signs and access rules.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Soft overcast days also suit the walls and courtyards well.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (inside the Grand Courtyard, facing the St John's Church facade and bell tower). The church facade and bell tower framed by the arcaded courtyard, with the observatory tower and its zodiac frieze in view. Walk a little closer along the way to find clean frames of the façades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so pale stonework keeps its texture and the sky does not wash out. In shaded courtyards, tap on a darker area instead and let the phone brighten the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines so they stay straight. Include an archway, passage or a person at the edge of the frame to give a sense of scale. Take one wide shot and one close detail shot of each part you like.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the buildings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want a whole façade or courtyard in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details and for pulling distant doorways or windows closer.

spots.name: Gediminas' Tower
spots.label: Gediminas' Tower

text.directions_text: Head for Gediminas Hill in Vilnius, close to the Royal Palace of Lithuania at its foot. The hilltop can be reached on foot or by lift, so choose whichever suits you. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Gediminas' Tower stands on top of Gediminas Hill in Vilnius, overlooking the Old Town. The rebuilt Royal Palace of Lithuania is near the base of the hill.
text.description:
Gediminas' Tower is the surviving part of the Upper Castle, standing on top of Gediminas Hill above Vilnius Old Town. It is a short, sturdy brick tower of three storeys, and it has become a symbol of both the city and Lithuania. It appeared on the old litas currency, and the national flag was raised on it again on 7 October 1988. The first wooden fortifications here are linked to Grand Duke Gediminas, and the first brick castle was finished in 1409 under Grand Duke Vytautas. The tower you see today was rebuilt in 1933.

It photographs well for two reasons. The tower itself makes a strong, simple shape against the sky, and the hilltop gives you a lift above the rooftops of the Old Town. The viewing platform also looks towards the modern business district, so one visit gives you both an old and a new Vilnius in the frame.

The phone icon on the map is right at the tower, so this is the place for close shots of the brickwork and the walls, and for looking out from the hill. Take a few steps back along the hilltop to fit the whole tower in, then go up to the platform for the panorama. Wipe your lens first, as phones pick up smudges easily, and keep your thumb clear of the edges when shooting wide.
text.access_note: The tower houses a museum and the hilltop can be reached on foot or by lift, so check the official site before you go for access to the tower and the viewing platform.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening usually gives softer, warmer light on the brick. Earlier in the day or on weekdays the hilltop is likely to be quieter.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the tower is right beside you, so you can shoot its walls and the view out over the city. For a full-length shot of the tower, step back along the hilltop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. For the wide view over the city, try panorama mode and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower's vertical edges parallel to the vertical grid lines. When shooting upwards, don't tilt the phone too far, or the walls will lean inwards. From the platform, put the Old Town rooftops in the lower third and leave the sky above. Choose one clear subject, such as a spire or a distant street, rather than trying to fit everything in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for close shots looking up at the tower. Use the default lens (1x) for the tower with some sky around it and for general views from the hilltop. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Old Town roofs and towers from the platform.

spots.name: Church of St. Johns, Vilnius
spots.label: St. Johns' Church

text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Vilnius Old Town and find Pilies gatvė. Šv. Jono gatvė is the small side street off it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Vilnius, within the Vilnius University ensemble. The viewpoint is on the small Šv. Jono gatvė, which runs off Pilies gatvė.
text.description: St John's is the big Baroque church at the heart of the Vilnius University buildings in the Old Town, and its white bell tower is the real star for photographs. The tower is 69 metres tall, which makes it the tallest building in the Old Town, so it shows up above the rooftops from many streets. The church itself is older than its looks suggest. A Gothic parish church was finished here in the 1420s. After a fire in 1737 the architect Johann Christoph Glaubitz gave the front the flowing, wavy lines now seen as typical of Vilnius Baroque, and the tower was raised higher at the same time. The Jesuits received the church in 1571, and it became part of the university that grew from their college. It still hosts services in Lithuanian and concerts. For a phone photo, the challenge is height: the tower and church sit close together among narrow streets, so you need to tilt your view upwards without losing the shape. Stand in the street, find the tower rising behind the church's side, and use the gridlines to keep the edges upright. Move a few steps until the tower sits clear of wires and signs. If you want a second shot, the university courtyard shows the main front and tower together, and Pilies gatvė shows the side of the church along the old street.
text.access_note: The street is open public space, but the church is a place of worship, so dress modestly and be quiet if you go in. Check the official site before you go for entry to the church, courtyard access and the bell tower, which is closed from roughly late October to April.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sky is bright but the street is not crowded; early morning is usually quieter. Soft, even light on a bright overcast day suits the pale tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Šv. Jono gatvė. The bell tower rising from the street, seen from the side with the church alongside it. Stand on Šv. From here the bell tower rises straight up from the street, seen from the side with the church alongside it. The church is a short step to the north. Vilnius University Great Courtyard is an alternative: the Baroque front of the church is on one side, with the tall tower beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the white walls keep their detail. Hold the phone level to avoid a leaning tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean. Keep some street at the bottom so the tower looks like it rises from it. For an alternative, Pilies gatvė shows the church's southern side, with its surviving Gothic windows, along the old street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower and the church together in a narrow street. If you can step back, try the default lens (1x) for a more natural shape. The telephoto (2x-5x) is good for the top of the tower.
